Mr. Speaker, may I just say a word on this, because last year I took part in discussions with Your Honour between the parties regarding the parking privileges, or the parking arrangements, on parliament hill.
Finally, it should be understood that while the Department of Public Works makes the over-all regulations with regard to traffic, including parking, on government property, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are then responsible for enforcing those regulations, nevertheless the Department of Public Works and certainly the R.C.M.P. recognize that although the precincts outside are not directly within the control of the house, nevertheless parliament itself has an overriding interest in the parking arrangements which are made on parliament hill. Therefore the matter of allocating spaces on the hill has always been discussed with and between the parties, as I understand it. Certainly this is the principle we like to follow and followed last year-that it is then for the Speaker and the Sergeant-at-Arms as a result of such discussion to determine what particular allocations of space will be made.
As far as I am aware there was no change in the allocation of spaces this year. Therefore I am not aware whether any spaces formerly allotted to visitors to members of parliament have been withdrawn. It seems to me that what is necessary if there is dissatisfaction with the allocation of parking space is that the parties should again meet with Your Honour and the Sergeant-at-Arms to discuss what changes or revisions, if any, should be made.

10. Agricultural Stabilization Act administration, $315,130.

Mr. Chairman, as I started to say last evening, the stabilization board has done a great service for the farmers of Canada generally and particularly for those in western Canada in whom I am greatly interested. Last year saw a record number of hogs sold, second only to the year 1942. In some manner or other we were able to handle a large number of hogs and store the surplus, and now we are getting rid of the surplus. In 1942, the only other year that compares with last year, Great Britain had a great demand for hogs. During the war we exported hogs to Great Britain in considerable quantities.
Last fall the stabilization board was of great assistance to the sheep industry when

lambs had to be supported, largely due to the scrapies disease that afflicted some of the western flocks, when some of the states south of the border placed an embargo on lambs going into that country. What would have been the price of lambs last autumn had there not been a support price? I think chaos would have reigned in the sheep industry. I know that neighbours of mine who sold lambs were greatly worried. In my opinion the stabilization board played a vital role in supporting the lamb market last year, and I was pleased to note that this support cost the board only $360,000.
As I mentioned last evening the hon. member for Assiniboia made no recommendation as to how to improve conditions or provide support for deficiency payments. His main argument was on behalf of the large producer. I think it is evident that the deficiency payment is made on hogs particularly to assist the small producer. I have always advocated deficiency payments on hogs and did so a year ago before the government brought them into effect. The small producer receives as much benefit as the large producer, and that is perhaps the way it should be. Surely the small producer has a right to as much support from the federal treasury as does the larger producer.
The hon. member for Assiniboia went on at great length to tell us how disappointed he was in the Conservative party, and how at one time he had great hopes for it because of the young members who were elected in 1957 and 1958. He did not say what hopes he had for his new labour party, of which he has become a member. He did not say that the Saskatchewan government has not adopted the labour party; he shied completely away from that.
He says he is disappointed in some of the Conservative members. I am disappointed in him as representing a rural riding of farmers. I am afraid he has sold them down the river to the labour party, which is controlled by unions in the United States. This is what has happened, and this is what is concerning farmers. He has joined a party which is dominated by international unions in the United States. He has sold the farmers down the river, and the Saskatchewan government has realized that fact and is playing safe until after the election of June 8.
I am told that somewhere around 85 per cent of the producers of hogs sell only 100 or fewer than 100 grade A and B hogs in a year. Eighty five per cent of all hogs sold grade A and B; therefore it is evident that by far the majority of the small producers particularly are being supported by this present stabilization method. The only ones
Supp ly-A griculture
that I could see it would hurt would be some of the larger producers whom my hon. friend from Assiniboia is attempting to support.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska said that hog exports had fallen 30 per cent. I am looking at the livestock trade report put out by the Department of Agriculture for the week ended May 12. Exports of live hogs to the United States are more than double those from January 1 to May 7 of last year. I am quoting from page 13 of this report. Live hogs exported to the United States this year ran over 3,300; last year they were around 1,400. On the same page we find the pork exports. They may be down 3 million, but a little further along I notice that canned meat is up over 6 million. Without doubt a great deal of canned meat consists of pork, and I would say that roughly our pork exports are holding at about the same level as last year, and certainly are not down 30 per cent. Where the hon. member got this figure I do not know.
He said that the main object of the stabilization board appears to be to reduce the surplus. It would be easy for the stabilization board to reduce the surplus. All they would need to do would be to do away with support altogether. If that was the main object of the government they could bring in a measure that would do away with support of hogs altogether, if the object was to reduce the surplus. Certainly surpluses have to be managed. The money from the federal treasury has to go to the small producers, or those who are in trouble. Certainly it is the small producer who needs the financial backing, and he is entitled to as much assistance as the large producer.
As I said, I have always advocated a deficiency payment plan on hogs. Perhaps it should have been initiated before the support price was lowered to 80 per cent of the 10-year average. I hope the minister and the government will see fit to make a semiannual payment on hogs. The farmers of western Canada particularly are accustomed to interim payments and final payments on their grain. We have been paid our deficiency payment on a half-yearly basis, and I hope the government will see fit to make a semiannual payment, perhaps on July 1 of every year, on hogs.
I say this because as a farmer I know that a few years ago when I started out farming, in the middle of July I allowed an insurance agent to sell me an insurance policy which cost me $50. For the next six or seven years, whenever the insurance premium came due, I was broke, and I received notice after notice from the insurance company asking me to please send in my money or they would have to revoke the policy. It was always

Supply-Agriculture
after about the very last notice in September that I seemed to be able to scrape up enough money to meet the insurance premium.
It is in the spring and summer that the farmer is hard pressed for cash. I urge the government to consider this and make the deficiency payment on hogs on a semi-annual basis. The minister said it would amount to only $2 or $2.10 at the present time, but $2 each on 50 hogs in the middle of the year, assuming that the farmer sold 50 hogs in the first half of the year and 50 in the second half, would amount to perhaps $100, which would go a long way toward keeping the farmer mobile and in a position to pay his bills throughout the summer. As I said, this would be welcomed by the farmers and particularly the small farmers who are producing a small number of hogs and are perhaps faced with a great many financial difficulties at that time and cannot wait until January for the money for their hogs. It seems difficult for them to wait until next January to get deficiency payment assistance.
I know full well there may not be any payments next year because the price of hogs may come up high enough to raise the level. If this is so the government should raise the support level. I would like to see it come up, because the small producer needs this assistance. I hope we have enough of a surplus by the end of this year so we can increase the support level to where it was, namely 84 per cent, rather than the mandatory level of 80 per cent.
This is about all I have to say on the stabilization board. It has been of great service to the farmers. Since the March 31, 1958 election, referred to by the hon. member for Assiniboia, the farmers have begun to realize just what a good act it is and just how much it will support them in case of a sudden drop in prices such as in the case of lambs, which occurred last fall in western Canada. The stabilization board has been of great benefit to the farmers and I hope it continues to be of service to them for a good while in the future.

I rise at this time, Mr. Chairman, to answer some of the statements made by the hon. member for Acadia. I said in my speech a week ago I felt that the government premise on which this act was based was exceedingly shaky; that the government in fact was not carrying out the act as required; that instead of bringing in a type of deficiency payment the government in fact was robbing the farmers of the support price they had.

Only the large
farmer.

Robbing all the farmers, robbing every single hog producer it could- and it will do it-every single hog producer who has sold hogs far below the so-called stabilization price; because any deficiency payment that is made will be inadequate and will not be enough to bring up the lowest prices that have been paid to the producer to the so-called support level.
To that extent the government, I suggest, is breaking its own act. It has considered this act to be no more than a piece of paper, which it is tearing up in the eyes of producers, certainly in my view based on the clauses in the act, based on the statements made by the minister and government supporters in the past. In reading the act I see nothing in it to suggest that the 80 per cent price over a period of years is not to be maintained as a firm price by way of return to the producers on all of the commodities that have been covered. But this is not the case; this is not what the government is doing under the act, and I feel that the farmers are not getting what they are entitled to under this legislation.
During the past winter the federation of agriculture presented a brief on this subject to the government and to other members of the House of Commons, and in it they came out very strongly in favour of the offer to purchase method. When Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner was minister of agriculture I suggested that the farmers did not in every single instance receive the prices to which they were entitled under the offer to purchase method, but I have no hesitation in saying that they received a far larger share of the support price than under this legislation, which is robbing them of their just due. The hon. member for Acadia went far afield from this stabilization item-
No farther afield than you.
-and in addition to some rather insulting and abusive remarks-
Oh, terrible.
-he made statements that were most unparliamentary.
You are one to talk.
He suggested that I had sold the farmers down the river-
Hear, hear.
-to some so-called labour party that is merely a figment of the hon. member's imagination.
What do you call it?
He knows so little about these developments that he does not know it is not going to be and will not be a labour party, and the people who are most determined-
Order.

Mr. Chairman, I can answer the hon. gentleman who made these statements. This party for which we have been working will not be a labour party, and the people who are most determined to see that it will not be a labour party are the trade union members themselves.
Controlled by American labour racketeers.

I did not hear that remark; perhaps the hon. member would like to repeat it. I heard something about labour racketeers. It will be very interesting to see these comments on the record made by hon. members who are attempting to malign the leadership of the trade union movement in this country.
No, not in this country.

The hon. member for Acadia said I had sold the farmers down the river to a labour party comprising trade unions that, in his words, would be controlled by Americans. This is an old tactic. It is not a new tactic, but the old tactic of smear and divide and rule if you can. I was sorry to hear a very active member of the Conservative party use this occasion to try to drive a wedge between the farming people and the workers in other industries in this country.
You have already driven a wedge.
This man is trying to stir up one class against another, and I think that is an abominable thing for anyone to do.
What are your C.C.F. members doing?

I will take a back seat to no one as a champion of the rights of the farmers of this country, but in doing that I do not have to malign and smear trade union members or the labour movement of this country. In addition to a very large body of farmers in my constituency, I have the honour and privilege of representing many people who work in stores, garages, hospitals and the sodium sulphate plants in my riding, and who are members of the trade union movement. I think these people are just as honourable, just as honest and just as good Canadian citizens as any member of this house, and they will resent the implication by the hon. member for Acadia that they are being controlled by gangsters from outside this country.

It is very interesting to hear hon. members say "order". As a member of the house I have a right to reply to the statements which have been made. I agree that they were out of order, but as they have been made I have a right to reply to them. The hon. member said that I have sold the farmers down the river. I challenge him and I challenge the Minister of Agriculture, as I have on other occasions, to appear with me on a public platform anywhere in western Canada to discuss the government's agricultural policy, the way the minister has endeavoured to hoodwink the farmers of this country and how he has failed to carry out the promises of the government to bring about parity prices and adequate support legislation. I know the minister will not accept my challenge, because he is too timid to face the agricultural producers of western Canada and take part in a public debate to discuss the way the government has mismanaged the stabilization legislation, and how it has been instrumental in driving down the prices of eggs and hogs.
After his initial tirade the hon. member for Acadia got around to saying something about improvements that could be made in the act. Everything the government was doing was fine until he got around to talking about the act itself, and then he thought there were many things wrong with it. He suggested that there should be semi-annual payments on hogs because he knows, and he said so, that if the price of hogs should go up toward the end of the year then, on the statement of the minister, the farmers may be deprived of a deficiency payment even though their hogs have sold at far below the so-called stabilization price.
I suggest that what the farmers need and have a right to is a daily and individual accounting with respect to the prices at which they sell their products; and whenever the price of a single hog or a single dozen of eggs falls below the stabilization price the farmer who has sold the eggs or the hog should have the right to the difference between the stabilization price established under this legislation and the market price. This is the difference, Mr. Chairman, from the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board Act under which, when the initial prices and initial grades are established, there is a guarantee without qualification that when a farmer markets a certain grade and quantity of grain he will receive the basic initial payment. There is no such guarantee in this legislation. There is no guarantee in this legislation whatsoever. The farmers are

Supply-Agriculture
thrown on the mercy of the market, and if the farmers are taken to the cleaners completely the minister may then by his own formula give them some little hand-out after their products have been marketed.
Under the legislation we are now discussing the farmer cannot say, because no one can say, what his rights are having regard to the manner in which the government is administering the support legislation. Although farmers have sold hogs this year, some of them have informed me, for as low as 18 cents, 17 cents or 16 cents a pound, they have no assurance, and the minister will not give them any assurance now, that he will pay to them the difference between the price they received, which was well below the stabilization price, and the stabilization price.
This is a hit-or-miss method as far as the farmer is concerned. The main objective of the minister is to clean up the surplus, clean up the inventories and drive the farmers out of the production of hogs, drive the farmers out of the production of eggs, liquidate the farmers so far as being producers is concerned, because that is exactly what the minister is doing. Then he will say, "My legislation has been a great success. I have moved the surplus products, and this is the main thing I should be considering in connection with my legislation". I do not believe this is a good thing. The producers are asking for equity; they are asking for fair treatment; they are asking that the formula in this legislation be maintained and that they be not chiselled by the administration of this act.
Chiselled?
Do you want something stronger than "chiselled"? I think it has been stolen.
Stolen?
They have taken from them the thing they have a right to expect; and because of the statements made by hon. members opposite when this legislation was being put through this house-
Why did you vote for it?
There is a brilliant question from my hon. friend.
Well, you did.

Oh, I did, yes; in spite of the fact that my hon. friend and others wanted to twist the position we had taken in connection with the bill. We had a little more faith in the government at that time than we have now. We thought that when the bill was drafted in clear and precise English

terms, the government would carry out the provisions of the legislation. We thought this was better than no legislation at all. We still have-
You would vote against it today, then?

-in our memory the ringing declaration of the Prime Minister that his policy for agricultural producers was parity, not charity. Well, the parity has been forgotten. It went out the window when the Prime Minister got this tremendous majority in the house. Even by way of charity there is little going to the agricultural producers at this time.
I did not intend, Mr. Chairman, to reenter the debate on this subject at this time. However, the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia, in which he endeavoured to set one occupational group against another, were of a character that should be answered.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that I should say something at this time, in view of the tub-thumping political speech which the hon. member for Assiniboia has just delivered, and which is a repetition of one he delivered last Friday. In each case his statement was full of inaccuracies, and took no cognizance whatever of the practical situation in this country so far as the production and marketing of agricultural products are concerned. These statements, as I say, were intended purely for political consumption and really have nothing to do with these estimates or an examination of these estimates.
The hon. member for Assiniboia repeated today what he said last Friday, that the act is not being followed in so far as the provision of support at the mandatory 80 per cent level is concerned. This is completely incorrect. We are providing support at the mandatory 80 per cent.
Not to the farmer.

Yes, we are providing it to the farmer. The hon. member and many other people have been going about this country talking about eggs at 15 cents and hogs at 16 cents, and various other figures along that line. In every case they have been picking out the lowest price at which any product has been sold at any time in Canada during the past several months. Then they say that is the price they are getting for their product. They say nothing about the fact that we have in effect the support price which is going to give to the farmers across this country the average support price. The support price provided for hogs, which is the average for Canada, is of course $22.65.

The hon. member and other hon. members who are talking for political purposes are only trying to stir up trouble. They omit to say that this support price is guaranteed to these farmers. What the hon. member is actually doing is constantly saying that we should have continued the support by means of purchase; and so are hon. members of the Liberal party. They say we should have continued the support by means of purchase, which was the method being carried on previously and which resulted in an accumulation of surplus products. The hon. member has asked a series of questions as to the prices paid for these products, and I shall proceed to answer them shortly. I hope the answer will present a complete picture and show how utterly impossible it was to continue support by the purchase method for a product such as hogs.
I wonder if the minister would permit a question.
Just a minute; I should like to finish what I am saying. The hon. member for Assiniboia and hon. members of the Liberal party can talk about supporting these products by the method of purchase-
Offer to purchase.

-or offer to purchase, whatever you like to call it. It is actually by making a purchase that you support the price. Their thinking is 20 years out of date; that is what is wrong with it. They leave out of consideration entirely the growth of contract farming and the integrated operations which have taken place in this country in recent years, and which were going on very rapidly, so far as hog production was concerned, when we stopped it by putting the deficiency payment method of support into operation. As a result of the hog contracts which were being made and as a result of the big integrated operations which were taking place, the production of hogs was zooming up and up. If we had continued the offer to purchase method of support that production would have continued to zoom, and it would have been impossible to handle the product.
Under those circumstances it was absolutely essential that we change the method of support so that we could support all the bona fide farmers, but cut out from support those people who were contract farmers, many of them businessmen who were going into this type of operation because they had a guaranteed profit from the government on it.
The hon. member for Assiniboia and hon. members of the Liberal party, in continuing to insist that we should have in effect the 79951-0-258i
Supply-Agriculture
offer to purchase method of support, are actually insisting we should continue to use the taxpayers' money to support the large commercial operations.
That is not true. That is a false and ridiculous statement.

That is the actual fact. This self-styled defender of the small man, the small farmer, is actually insisting on a course of action which will support the large commercial farmers, the big feed companies, the abattoirs and people engaged in this kind of contract farming.
I rise on a question of privilege.
Take your medicine on the chin.

My question of privilege is that the Minister of Agriculture is putting words in my mouth which have never been there. He is giving a false statement. I have never at any time breathed one word of support in this house for the great corporations engaged in agriculture production, for the integrated farm or anything else. I have been an opponent of vertical integration, and I still am.

I think you realize, Mr. Chairman, that this is a completely false question of privilege. There is no question of privilege involved. The hon. member is trying to say I did something that I did not do. What I said was, and I repeat, that by trying to insist that we keep in effect the offer to purchase method, he is in effect-these were the words I used-asking us to support the large commercial concerns to the detriment of the small farmer. That is exactly the situation.
In effect you are not telling the truth.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask that you have that remark withdrawn immediately. The hon. member has said, "You were not telling the truth".

speechtext: Order. I heard the words used. I think the expression is unparliamentary, and I am sure the hon. member for Skeena will withdraw it.
Save it for television.
Withdraw.

I am sure the hon. member for Skeena would not care to withdraw what he said. What I said was "In effect the minister is not telling the truth". If the minister can use the expression "in effect" to introduce words which were never uttered by the hon. member for Assiniboia, then

Supply-Agriculture
anybody else has the right to do precisely the same thing. I know what I say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary to discuss the explanation of the hon. member. What I was mentioning to him was the fact that under our standards the expression he used should be withdrawn. I am sure that on reflection he will withdraw it.

If I may speak to the point of order again, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we went through this situation with the same minister and myself a couple of years ago with regard to a somewhat similar expression. Even though I said that in effect the minister was not telling the truth, there is a vast difference between saying a person is not telling the truth and saying that he is telling a lie. I did not say that the minister was telling a lie.
Oh, oh.
There is a distinct difference there.
Will you explain it?
Certainly I will explain it.
It does not require any explanation.

One of your colleagues over here asked for an explanation. Why do you people not keep in concert with each other? It is unparliamentary to say that a person is telling a lie because this is saying that he knows precisely what he is saying and that he is lying deliberately, is telling a falsehood, is distorting what I have been saying. But to say that a person is not telling the truth is namely saying in effect that he does not know what he is talking about.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. May I suggest to the hon. member, as one who occupies a neutral position in this situation, that he really ought to withdraw the words to which objection has been taken. I think he will find that such words have been interpreted by previous Speakers as being offensive and unparliamentary. In fairness to the hon. member-and I know he does not mean to violate the rules-may I suggest that he might use a more effective synonym and say that the Minister of Agriculture is guilty of a terminological inexactitude.

Speaking on the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I could not accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Essex East either. We know how smooth, capable and mellifluous he is in his ability to get around difficulties, to say one thing

and put it in different words so the statement does not sound quite so offensive. What I said is quite true, Mr. Chairman; but on your insistance that this expression be withdrawn because it casts a reflection on the minister, I will withdraw it to that extent.
You are defying the Chair.
I am not defying the Chair. I have just said that I withdraw it. Does the hon. member not pay attention to what is going on?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the incident can be considered as closed. I thank the hon. member for Skeena for withdrawing the expression.

Mr. Chairman, I was just speaking of the really untenable position of the hon. member for Assiniboia and members of the Liberal party in continuing to insist that we should continue with the offer to purchase method of support of perishable products such as hogs, eggs and so on which can be produced in extremely large quantities. A system of that sort, of course, for those products encourages contract farming, integrated operations and so on which produce a quantity of these products which you just cannot handle. The offer to purchase method really comes down to this situation. You are using a great deal of the taxpayers' money to support people who are not farmers at all, or are not bona fide farmers, and there is no justification for using the taxpayers' money for this purpose.
Under the system we have in effect for both hogs and eggs there is real protection for farmers. In the case of hogs, something over 90 per cent of the hog producers- that is practically all the bona fide farmers -are fully protected on the prices of the A and B hogs which they deliver. All those farmers across Canada will get on the average the support price we have guaranteed. If the price they actually receive does not come to that amount, we will make a deficiency payment in order to make up the difference.
The hon. member was complaining that these payments are not on an individual daily basis. This would be a completely hopeless operation. The cost would be away out of reason. In addition to that consideration it just is not workable anyway, because then there would be no incentive to the individual farmer to get the best price possible for his hog or his group of hogs, and it would lead to one of the worst black markets that ever existed in this or any other country. It just is not a practical proposition from any point of view.

The hon. member advocates things along that line because he has no business experience and no practical experience in administration. He does not understand what he is advocating when he advocates these things.
The wheat board can do it.

It is very easy for wild theorists to advocate all kinds of things, but most of the things they advocate are just not practicable or workable. That is the situation with regard to many of the things advocated by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
The hon. member went on to say that we are trying to liquidate the farmers as producers. The whole purpose of this scheme is to protect the bona fide farmer and to get the non-farmer-the businessman, the contract man, the feed company and so on- out of the production of hogs and eggs and other products.
The hon. member quoted the federation of agriculture and tried to make out that they were unanimously against this system and in favour of the offer to purchase system, something which does not happen to be the case. Some of the member bodies of the federation are certainly in favour of the offer to purchase system, particularly the ones that are dominated by the big producers. But he said nothing about the farm unions, who endorse this method of support. As a matter of fact he is generally quoting the farm unions here, but in this case he did not mention anything about them because he knows they support the deficiency method of payment in order to prevent what I have just been talking about, namely the growth of contract farming, integrated operations and so on. Hence this statement that we are trying to liquidate the farmers is the exact opposite of the case. We have put this type of support into operation for the specific purpose of protecting the bona fide farmer and preventing competition with him on the part of big business concerns.
As far as these general statements along that line are concerned, I think that is all the time I will take in order to deal with them at the present moment. There is just one other thing. The hon. member for Assiniboia stated that under the previous government the method of support in operation was much more advantageous to the farmers than is the case under the stabilization act.
No.

If the hon. member says he did not say that, well and good. What did he say along this line?
Supply-Agriculture
I said the farmers got a higher proportion of the support level for their products than they get under this act.

I do not know what the hon. member means when he says they got a higher proportion of the support level, but here are the actual figures of what they got. For the 12 years the Liberals were operating the Agricultural Prices Support Act the farmers got a total of approximately $24 million in payments under that act, except for hogs and cattle during the period of foot-and-mouth disease, when special measures were taken. A great deal of pork was canned at that time, and so forth. That canning and support program during the foot-and-mouth outbreak amounted to $36.6 million for hogs and $33.3 million for cattle. But apart from those special measures to meet the foot-and-mouth outbreak the total amount which the farmers received in 12 years under the Liberals was $24 million.
That was taken out of the treasury.

Mr. Chairman, in the last year alone we expended $57.6 million. That is in one year alone, as compared with $24 million in 12 years; yet the hon. member says that under the previous government the farmers got more support than under this government. The figures themselves show how ridiculous is a statement like that, and every farmer in the country knows that is the situation. There is just no use arguing about the figures, because they speak for themselves.
As far as the argument the hon. member now makes is concerned, namely that they get a lot of other indirect support because the money was put out by the treasury, that is correct. It is correct now, it was correct then and it has been correct right through. As I pointed out last Friday, the actual amount of money which the treasury puts out is no measure of the amount of benefit for the farmers. I indicated some figures last Friday to illustrate that point so far as the dairy industry was concerned, and I will not repeat them again. But that statement applies now just as it did before. These figures actually indicate the disparity in support as between what was provided under the Liberal government and what has been provided under this government, and as I say there is no comparison.
Some questions were asked which I was requested to answer today. First of all the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska asked about pork imports into Canada from the United States since the lifting of the

Supply-Agriculture
embargo. Fresh pork, which includes trimmings, amounted to 1,067,000 pounds. In addition there was pickled and cured pork to Newfoundland, 691,000 pounds. That has been going on for years and is a well established trade. I might point out that the weekly kill during recent weeks has been running better than 21 million pounds a week. Information also is that the imports which were made were not successful financially, and repeat orders have not been going forward.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska also asked for the number of farmers who had registered for deficiency payments for hogs, and the number is 180,420. I have the figures broken down into provinces but I will not give them all unless he asks for them. I will give him the figure for Quebec, and that is 27,382.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska asked another question last night which I was not able to catch on the translation system. However, it appears in Hansard in this form as reported on page 2 of the translation:
Could the minister tell us whether legal action was taken against farmers who took advantage of the Agricultural Stabilization Act trader two registration numbers?
I stated some time ago that certain farmers were using two registration numbers. Therefore, I ask the minister whether legal action was taken by the Department of Agriculture.
At the time the hon. member brought this up I first of all asked him if he knew of any cases of this kind, to give me the names of the people concerned and I would take immediate action. I have not received the names of anybody concerning this matter. Naturally I cannot send police officers around to investigate all the farmers in Canada. That is not a practical proposition, and in any event I would not do it. If a farmer had a police officer or some other investigator come around to his place and ask him a lot of questions as to whether he had two registration numbers or whether he was conniving with somebody else and having that somebody else use his registration number, then I think that farmer would have justifiable grounds for complaint. But if the hon. member, or if any other hon. member, can give me any specific case where they have reason to believe this practice is going on, we will deal with it, because we are most anxious to see the practice stopped.
The hon. member for Assiniboia asked me a lot of questions about statistical information. I now have that information here and am prepared to give it.
This is with regard to the purchase of pork?
Yes.
In Alberta?
This is not Alberta; this is Canada.
I thought the question dealt with Alberta.

As long as producers provide their creamery with a top grade cream and creameries do a good job, there is no excuse for turning out butter

The removal of the support price on eggs, replaced by deficiency payments, is supposed, in the long run, to benefit the poultry industry, it is said. But tell me, since when is it consistent with morals to allow the patient to die in order to cure his ills?
That sudden reversal of policy, without our being given the least chance to prepare for it, has not only removed our benefits completely but has forced us to spend money which is now impossible for us to earn if we want to keep operating from day to day. No income of any kind, for family expenses, while we are forced to resort to credit to pay the cost of operations.
We are worse off than during the great depression years of the thirties. At least, at that time we were all in the same boat. We could hire a man at $15 a month in summer, and $5 a month in winter, and a servant at $8 or $10, who still knew they were lucky to have at least a place to hang up their hats.
And it was the same with the rest, besides the fact that it was still possible to keep out of debt if we really wanted to. But the labour market is no longer at that level. Today, we have to face competition from a high-pressure economy you are so fond of boasting about, and our costs remain at top levels.

In connection with the
question raised by the hon. gentleman, the number of egg producers registered is 89,545.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, that figure therefore represents about 25 per cent of Canada's poultry farmers.
Now, when the minister amended his methods, he said 90 per cent of the poultry farmers would benefit from the new price support system. Moreover, it must be remembered that those poultry producers who have registered will get price support on only 1,000 dozens. What we would have liked to know, therefore, was what proportion of egg production would qualify under the agricultural price support legislation.
This is only my own deduction, of course, but I think less than 5 per cent of Canada's egg production will qualify for deficiency payments.

Mr. Chairman, I have been following closely the remarks made a moment ago by my hon. friend from Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). As I understand his remarks, he has said that Canadian farmers were not satisfied with the Agricultural Stabilization Act, indeed that they were dissatisfied with it.
No, that is not what he said.
Mr. Chairman, I am not surprised at this interjection from the hon. member for Essex East, because he has been prompting his colleague all along, as the latter is unable to speak for himself.
The hon. member should withdraw that statement. He knows quite well that the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska is an expert on agricultural matters.

This is particularly obvious by the way he talks.
Mr. Chairman, I have been wondering whether the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska has any authority to speak on behalf of the farmers of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman is stating that the hon. member from Drummond-Arthabaska has no right to speak on behalf of the farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I did not say that the hon. member had no right to speak on behalf of the farmers of Canada. What I said is that the hon. gentleman has no authority to do so.
What about you?

All right, I will stand up.

speechtext:
Order. The Chair recognizes the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.
(Translation):

If I may, Mr. Chairman, I shall go on with my remarks, in spite of interjec-
Supp ly-A griculture
tions from the opposition benches, and say that farmers, more particularly in our part of the country-for I do not hesitate to say this of all farmers in the province of Quebec, and throughout Canada-are satisfied with the Agricultural Stabilization Act which this Conservative government introduced to provide farmers with the fair share of income to which they are entitled.
I have here, Mr. Chairman-and I had to go and fetch it in all haste-some excerpts from the press to prove my arguments. For instance, I have here an article published in Le Courrier of St. Hyacinthe of Thursday March 3, 1960, which reported on a meeting of members of the Canadian farmers' union (U.C.C.) in Granby, under the title:
Local fanners in favour of price support.
Mr. Chairman, if farmers did not favour the price support act, they would certainly not meet in a convention to ask the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for an extension of the legislation on price stabilization which was worked out and introduced in order to give our farmers what they are entitled to get.
I also have here another item from the same paper, dated December 10, 1959, which deals more particularly with the price support for beets. In that article we find that, for the riding of St. Hyacinthe, subsidies were $41,390.70, whereas, for the whole province of Quebec those grants were $73,039.99. If you wish, you may add the $4 million which went into the Quebec farmers' pockets in the form of a subsidy of 25 cents per hundredweight of milk, and you will get a very appreciable amount which our farmers were very pleased to receive and for which they commended and will continue to commend the government, which had the courage and vision to consider their interests.
I shall give you another irrefutable proof, from the very lips of the so-called expert on agriculture, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska. As we may see on page 2464 of the English text of Hansard, he said that for twelve years, under the Liberal administration, that is from 1946 to March 1957, the Agricultural Stabilization Act had brought the farmers he amount of $25,052,809-98. And he deplored the fact that this government had given farmers $78 million in the shape of grants.
Those people, Mr. Chairman, do not know when they should cry or laugh. They want to do both at the same time. And they think

Supply-Agriculture
that all the farmers are not bright enough to see through their game. They always want to play politics and that is why they are now out in the cold, on the opposition benches, where they will remain for a long time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to give a brief answer to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I said that the government had given $57 million last year and, $78 million during the two preceding years, that is, in 1957 and 1958. I do not remember-
That is what I said.
I stated that, during the last 12 years of Liberal rule, the government had given $24 million in deficiency payments to our farmers, at a time when farmers were selling their grain-
You deplore the fact that farmers had too much.

I can prove, Mr. Chairman, that even with the price support act, and with the amount of $57 million we disbursed last year, the farmers were not satisfied with the prices they had obtained. I have here a list of prices from 1947 to 1956-
You have so many of them that you get all mixed up.

The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe has a way, which I find it hard to describe, of distorting our arguments. But I know perfectly that he is in no position to tell me much about agriculture. From 1947 to 1956, in the last ten years of the Liberal regime, these were the prices paid to farmers for some of their products.
I have read them.
Wheat was selling at $1.49; under the Conservative regime, it was selling at $1.23.
You are comparing ten years with three years, the third to the whole.
From 1957 to 1959, the Liberal regime has given-
You are comparing ten years with three years.

Barley was selling at $1 a bushel from 1947 to 1956, under the Liberal regime, while Department of Agriculture was headed by the greatest minister of agricultural we have ever known; and it was

75 cents from 1957-1959. Oats was selling at
67.6	cents, while in 1957-1959, it was selling at 53 cents.
That is because of the surpluses you had piled up.
Flaxseed was selling at $3.62 under the Liberal regime, and at $2.67 under the Tory regime.
We had to get rid of your surpluses.

From 1947 to 1956, hogs were selling at $27.16 a hundredweight while from 1957 to 1959, they were selling at $26.19.
From 1947 to 1956, eggs were selling at
41.6	cents a dozen, and at 35 cents a dozen from 1957 to 1959.
If the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot wishes to obtain other figures, I am in a position to supply them to him.
You do not understand them, and that is the trouble.

The average price for the ten-year period preceding 1957, on which was the support price for hogs was based, was $28.40 the hundredweight, while in 1959, after three years of Tory regime, hogs were selling at $22.99.
As for the price of eggs, in 1959-
Give us also the prices of cheese and butter.
He just does not want to talk about those.
If you want me to talk about butter, I shall do so. Right now butter is selling at 64 cents a pound-
How much was it selling for under your administration?
Under the Liberal administration, it was about 58 cents a pound-*
And you say we reduced the price?
What about the price of cheese?

The price of butter has gone up. That, I admit, as I said the other day. Apparently, the hon. members were not in the house at the time. I said the price of butter had risen, and I explained why the present price of 64 cents a pound is worth no more than the 58 cent price a few years ago, because the index of production costs has risen tremendously. So if you want to compare the present price of butter, namely 64

cents a pound, with the price of a few years ago, butter would have to sell at 66 to 68 cents a pound.
Can you name one country where the price of butter is as high as in Canada?
It is not a matter of comparing Canada's farm prices with those of other countries. To do that, you would have-
Our production costs are not the same.
-to quote production costs. When we criticized the agricultural prices stabilization act, we were told it would protect farm income-
Then why did you vote for it?
-and as far as I know-
You supported it.

-the farmer's income has not been guaranteed, because his net income has dropped 7 per cent in 1959. That is an estimate, but when the revised figures come out-perhaps they are available by now- the drop will be 10 or 12 per cent.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are a few thoughts I wanted to submit to the house following the inappropriate remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot; should he need further information, I am prepared to supply it.

Mr. Chairman, this seems to me to be about the right time to get into this debate. I believe the people of Canada are very grateful to this government for what it has done. I can understand it is the duty of the opposition to criticize the government but let them take a realistic view and make a comparison beween world prices and what the farmers are receiving in Canada. Certainly we would all like to see an increase in the returns to our producers but we cannot control world conditions; we cannot control production.
We consider that the standard of living in the United States is high and possibly higher than ours. We have a reciprocal trade arrangement, and have had it for a number of years, under which we trade back and forth at set duty rates. Therefore, whether we like it or not, our market values are somewhat in line with theirs. It is only fair to make a comparison with the last four months period of 1959. If we do that we will find that the average price of good steers in the United States was $23.74 and in Canada $24.55, which shows that we are closely interrelated as far as prices are concerned.
Supply-Agriculture
In the last three months of 1959 the price of hogs in the United States was $16.43 dressed weight basis, whereas in Canada the national average was $23.67, which means that our price was $7 a hundred higher than the United States price. But, in 1952-our friends in the opposition will not say this -a disease broke out among hogs in the United States and the producers in that country were not allowed to send them into this country until that disease was cleared up. Permission was given to allow them in in the early part of 1960. On a reciprocal trade basis they were permitted to send pork products into Canada.
The United States is a country which raises 10 times as many hogs as we do and they can produce much more if they have to. Certainly, our prices are closely in line with theirs. The minister took the only sound approach that was possible or feasible and the figures he gave today as to exports and particularly with respect to hog bellies rendered into lard indicate that the returns were less than you would get for dog food. Is it logical or sound to waste the taxpayers' money to encourage overproduction, especially by commercial organizations, without in any way limiting the quantity that may be produced? I want to substantiate the minister's stand and I may say I have figures here for the Toronto market which after all is the largest market in Canada.
In the three months from October 1 to December 31, 1958, 95.75 per cent of the producers of hogs sold less than 50 hogs in that period of time which is the period of the year when there is the heaviest marketing. But when we take the total number of hogs that were put on the market we find that 70.4 per cent of the hogs were marketed by 95.75 per cent of the producers which proves beyond any question of doubt that during that period of time 4J per cent of the producers sold 30 per cent of the hogs. Is it sound judgment or good practice for the government to continue a policy that involves a guarantee to the owners of large piggeries who are perhaps making $8 to $10 a head and are raising as many as 8,000 to 10,000 hogs in the vicinity of Montreal or Toronto for marketing in those cities?
That was the situation, and I want to compliment the government and in particular the Minister of Agriculture who had the courage and conviction to try to protect the family farmer. Today in my constituency, as is the case elsewhere, 75 per cent of the farmers are men from 35 to 60 years of age with no more than ordinary academic training. If they and their families are forced off the farms they have no alternative but to go to industrial centres. We have a condition of

Supply-Agriculture
unemployment today and we will only be sending these people into misery and hardship. Therefore I repeat that the minister's stand was a courageous one and the only one that was feasible or sound in the face of the facts before him.
We do not hear too much criticism about beef because we are in a cycle of high prices but in a year or two from now when the United States starts to ship surplus cattle into this country we will be bound to feel the effects because their cattle population is ten times that of Canada. Therefore over the course of the years we are bound to feel the impact of that sooner or later.
As far as dairy products are concerned, our friends do not say very much about them because we guarantee 64 cents a pound for butter when there is no market in the world outside of Great Britain that will buy it at any price and Danish and New Zealand butter is being sold there today at 35 cents a pound. I ask the hon. member to name one market where we can sell any butter at the price that we guarantee in our home market. The same thing applies to cheese. I should like the hon. member for Essex East to stay here because he was one of the members of a cabinet that did not pay much attention to the cheese producers.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member, whom I hear speaking for the first time and who by the way declaims very well, if I may say so-I wish I could say the same thing about his argument-says that when I was in the cabinet nothing was done for the cheese producers of Canada. I want to let my hon. friend know that I was not aware that he was a member of the same cabinet or that he was clerk of council and was in a position to know what went on. I want my hon. friend to know, now that we have had an opportunity to compare the results of the present agricultural policy with the agricultural policy of the previous government
Order.

speechtext: Order.
-that there is no comparison with what the former government did.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I do not see
any point of order raised by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to give the hon. member every opportunity because the fact is that in the last six years his government was in power cheese prices held fairly well in Ontario thanks to the Ontario government which had to take over a second mortgage on the product in order to stabilize

it for the rest of Canada. Today we are receiving a fair return. I admit that we would certainly all like to see the farmers have a better living but on the basis of world prices, when New Zealand is selling cheese to Great Britain today at 23 or 24 cents a pound and having in mind that in Canada there is a guarantee equivalent to 32 cents a pound plus a subsidy of 25 cents per 100 pounds of milk or almost 35 cents altogether, I think our farmers are reasonably fair and appreciate that sort of protection. Certainly they never enjoyed it under the former government.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska put forward arguments on the basis of the period from 1947 to 1956. He failed to state that that was the aftermath of the war and that during that period we had to send our surplus production to countries which were demolished during the war. We also had the Korean war during that period of time. There was an altogether different position with respect to the disposition of surplus food stuffs. But the hon. member failed to tell about the mess they left which the present government inherited and the fact there were no markets available in which to sell our surpluses. It may comfort him to tell his side of the story. I suppose if I were in the opposition I would do the same thing, but nevertheless I believe in being fair. (Translation):
Last week, the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska made a comparison between the price on hogs in 1956 and in 1960. However, he forgot to check on his information beforehand, because in 1956 the average weekly production was about 115,000 hogs, while in the first three months of 1959 and 1960, production reached more than
164,000	hogs each week. Therefore, the present overproduction should be considered.
The hon. member did not say anything about the price of beef, nor about the price of butter and cheese; he preferred to mention only the price on hogs and eggs.
I congratulate the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for their efforts to protect the family farm. Before the year's end, I feel that it will be possible to establish an average production, thus enabling egg producers to get a higher income. Moreover, I am convinced that hog breeders will obtain a higher price, and before August, too.

Mr. Chairman, may I say just a few words following the remarks made by the member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Villeneuve). However, I do not want to disprove his remarks, which might take too long and, besides, I have already dealt with them. All I want to say is this. Members on

the government side say the farmer is satisfied with the agricultural acts which have been in force for some years, but I will simply quote from press reports which reflect the view of farmers and of farm representatives of the province.
I have here an excerpt from an article published in he Devoir of October 21 last, signed by Mr. Jean-Baptiste Lemoine, president of the Quebec Catholic union of farmers, who is recognized by all as an authority in the field of agriculture. Here is what he said:
We are walking in a fog, towards the unknown.
After writing about the Agricultural Stabilization Act, he said:
We are walking in a fog.
Here is the view of the Canadian federation of agriculture on that matter:
That legislation should not apply to products such as pork, beef, eggs and dairy products.
Furthermore, a supporter of this government, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) said the following, in this house:
If I understand the formula correctly, it is the most backward that could be adopted from an already established position.
And a little further on, he said:
I believe the program which has been announced and introduced destroys all hope in the production and sale of perishable goods. This program can only serve the opposite of the intended purpose. Instead of helping the small producers, it crushes them. It encourages speculators to play with the prices. It favours a lack of balance between supply and demand.
Mr. Chairman, before we carry this item, I would have to ask the Minister of Agriculture a few questions arising from an article published by the Ontario farmers union, of 1960. I would like to ask the minister to tell us if he confirms or denies this part of the article that I want to quote:
(Text):
According to the poultry products market report dated April 1, over 2,348,000 pounds of dressed poultry were imported into Canada in this first part of 1960. This is a million and a half pounds more than the same period of 1959. In spite of these figures, it is reported that prices have increased to the consumer from 37 or 38 cents a pound for turkeys to 56 cents.
(Translation):
Lately, there have been delegations of farmers calling to submit briefs to the Minister of Agriculture, and the matter of imports came up.
I should like the minister to tell us what has been the amount or value of our imports from January 1 to the latest date, as compared with the same period last year?
Supply-Agriculture
(Text):

In connection with that last figure, these figures appear every week in the poultry products market report. This report shows that dressed poultry imported up to May 14, 1960 was 1,942,580 pounds of chickens and in 1959, 449,140 pounds of chickens. In so far as turkeys are concerned, there were 1,151,000 pounds imported in 1960 and none in 1959.
I should like to point out to the hon. member that we do not have a closed border with the United States. During the time that we have been importing a few million pounds of poultry from the United States, we have been exporting to the United States very large quantities of cattle and hogs. No hon. member, of course, can expect that trade is going to be a one-way street.
(Translation):

This, of course, does not tally with the promises made by the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister in 1957 and 1958, to send out an army of salesmen in every country of the world to find markets for our products.
If our imports go on increasing all the time, I just wonder what will happen to the poultry farmer before very long. There is already some discrimination against poultry farmers in Canada, and unless imports are checked, our poultry farmers will be wiped out for good.
(Text):

I did not intend to take part in this debate at this time, but some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska should be corrected. He has been highly critical of the agricultural stabilization measure. He has not been the only one who has taken that view. I recall that in January, 1958, before the 1958 election, the hon. member for Assiniboia said that the agricultural prices stabilization measure would be the death warrant of the Conservative party. That prediction did not turn out to be very sound, and I do not believe the arguments presented by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska are any more sound.
This program is one of three particular projects which the government has adopted to deal with the problem of the fluctuation in farm income. The other two are the amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which have resulted in 10 per cent to 15 per cent more farmers benefiting from that legislation than formerly, and the crop insurance program under which the federal government has offered to pay 20 per cent of the cost of the premiums and 50 per cent of

Supply-Agriculture
the cost of administration, in addition to making loans to those provinces that take up the scheme.
The introduction of this agricultural prices stabilization act, as is well known, has resulted in the establishment of mandatory floor prices on nine commodities, with an additional dozen or so other agricultural products receiving support. In view of the remarks of the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska, and the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, I should like to put on the record the official views of the only farm organization in Canada which represents all farmers on a national scale. I refer to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which presented its views to the cabinet on February 24 of this year. This is what they had to say about price support:
We recognize that in present price support programs we have most of the fundamentals that we, as producers, have asked for and agreed are desirable.
That is the view of the only farm organization which represents the generality of farmers on a national scale. I think their views should be taken into consideration when discussing this particular item of legislation. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska made some comments about the level at which support prices should be maintained. I should like again to refer him to the presentation by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when they said that they recognized that supports which create and perpetuate surpluses cannot be satisfactory over a period of time.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska has been dealing with dairy price supports and with the butter support program. Surely it was welcome news to the farmers of this country and to the members of this house who are seriously concerned with the problems of agriculture and who, for example, take into account the views of the Ontario Rural Co-operator, when the minister announced in this house the establishment of the butter support price for this year. In their April 26 issue they carried this headline "Dairy Price Supports Welcome". They went on to say this:
The recently announced dairy policy for the 1960-61 production year must surely be welcome news for dairy farmers across Canada.
That is the view taken by responsible farm organizations in connection with this particular item which is under discussion at this time. I think those views are in direct refutation of the position which has been taken by the hon. member who has just been speaking. Coming from an area where poultry and eggs are raised not by large producers as the sole source of income but

as a necessary part of the farmers cash income, I can say that the egg support policy adopted by this government has proved to be satisfactory.
Some doubts were expressed at the initiation of this particular program. We were faced with a situation in which egg factories capable of mass production on a low cost basis were flooding the markets to the detriment of the small poultry raisers. With the introduction of this deficiency payment system providing for supports under the deficiency payments scheme on up to 4,000 dozen grade A large and extra large eggs, supports were provided to the farmers who needed them most, namely the great majority of the small egg producers. As must be apparent to everyone and as has been apparent to the egg producers themselves, under the previous system the production of eggs was being increased by what proved to be an incentive price and huge surpluses were being piled up for the benefit not of the ordinary egg producer but of the mass producer, the egg factory.
In conclusion may I say that from the approval given to the price support policy in general by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and others it is fairly evident that this act has worked out to the great benefit of Canadian farmers.

I just want to ask the minister two questions. Can he tell us again-he has probably given this information to other members-the difficulties, as he sees them, with regard to bringing pulpwood under this particular administration? The second question is this. Has he any figures at all that would indicate, on a regional basis, how much time and money handled by this administration has gone into the northwestern Ontario region?

As to the latter part of the question, may I say that we have no breakdown along that line for pulpwood. There are almost insuperable difficulties as far as bringing it under the act is concerned. If we attempt to purchase it under the act, we have no place to store it or anything else along that line. If we were paying a deficiency payment on it, it would really be a deficiency payment to a large extent to the large pulp and paper companies, which would enable them to get their wood at a lower price than they would be paying for it otherwise. Actually I think the best means of improvement along that line are the ones which have already been initiated by the pulp producers in forming their co-operative associations and as a result being in a better bargaining position to improve the price for their

pulpwood. This has already happened in a considerable number of places.

With regard to the pulp question, I know that in Quebec the provincial government has encouraged the formation of co-operatives by pulp producers. An attempt is being made to form one in our own region at the present time. I do not like to bring to the minister's attention campaign promises or election promises but strong indications were given by a number of ministers during the last campaign, and I would remind the ministers specifically of what the Prime Minister said in Rimouski, Quebec, prior to the last election. It seems to me that the whole movement on the part of the government has died almost of inanition.
I should like to know more about the difficulties than the minister has given us. How thoroughly did his department go into this question? The reason I raise the matter is that every farmer who cuts pulpwood is aware of the economic power of the people to whom he sells it. These are large corporations. I do not know of a group that in the main have had less co-operative experience and who have less pressure to exert in a political and economic way than have the bush farmers. Can the minister give us a little more explanation as to how much study his department and the government made of this matter, when it came to this decision and whether there are any steps it can take, in co-operation with the provincial governments, to improve the position?
The minister did not mention one weakness in trying to set up a scheme that is very apparent today, namely the regional nature of so much of the pulpwood market and the high cost of transportation. We have in northwestern Ontario a situation that I could point out to him in which pulpwood is coming down from northern Saskatchewan and from northern Manitoba all the way to mills at Fort Frances and Kenora, a fairly long transportation haul. One of the difficulties that is occasioned here is that the farmer in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba is in a position to take a much lower price than are the ones in northern Ontario. This is an example of an invasion of one group of farmers' pulp market by another region. I just wondered how much analysis went into this matter. Can I put on the order paper a request for papers and expect to get anything from the department?

We looked into this matter quite thoroughly. I do not think there are any papers particularly that I could produce in response to a request for the production of papers. The one definite step, of course, that was taken by the federal government to
Supp ly-A griculture
correct the situation was the prosecution of the paper companies for having a combine to depress the price paid to the farmers for pulpwood. That action, of course, resulted in a considerable improvement in the price in certain areas, combined with the formation of these co-operative pulp selling organizations by the farmers.
As I indicated previously, the practical difficulties in the way of providing price support for a commodity of this kind are extremely great. Indeed, it did not look as though it would be a practical proposition. Certainly on an offer to purchase program there was just no means that we had to handle the pulpwood; and on a deficiency payment basis, it created a situation in which it was just that much easier in a way for the paper companies to get away from pressure to increase their price for pulpwood. In effect, what we would have been doing by deficiency payments would have been to contribute to a considerable extent to the welfare of the paper companies which certainly do not need that sort of assistance from the general taxpayer.
For these various reasons, we did not consider that this was a practical means of dealing with the situation. We therefore went ahead with the combines investigation prosecution and we have been doing what we could to encourage the provincial governments and groups of farmers to form their own selling organizations.
I have one question. Does the minister's department consider pulpwood to be a farm product?

Strictly speaking, I do not know that you could consider it to be a farm product the same as, we will say, wheat, oats, barley or other products along that line. I do not know that there is in the act anything which would specifically exclude it. But certainly it is not a farm product in the same way as is a commodity such as the grains I have mentioned or livestock and so on.

The reason I raise this point is that under provincial legislation in Ontario it is possible under their marketing act to bring in pulpwood. However, there is one other factor. We have a pulp mill situation at the lakehead where all the big mills have large limits held from the crown; that is, the crown through the province of Ontario. At the same time each of these companies buys a considerable amount of pulpwood from what we call farmers, bush farmers, and this is a very important part of their income. Recently one of the companies in particular-there are others-has not only been importing wood from Manitoba and Saskatchewan, which is

Supply-Agriculture
after all an interprovincial matter and nothing that we can complain of, but it has also been importing in considerable quantities- at least, the value is up I believe over the $1 million mark-of pulpwood from the United States. It is really carrying coals to Newcastle in the minds of many people there.
What it is very difficult for us to do is to put our finger on someone who could be responsible. I see that the chairman is looking at me and I am probably getting somewhat away from this particular item, but I would like to have the minister's opinion whether it could properly be a matter of concern, if this product is a farm product, that United States competition is coming in into this particular market.

Mr. Chairman, all I can say is this. As I mentioned in connection with some other products, so far as imports from the United States are concerned we have a big two-way trade and we certainly export a great deal more in the way of pulp and paper products to the United States than the amount we import. The amount we import from them is comparatively negligible. As I have said before, we cannot expect to be able to carry on trade and have it flow all in the one direction as far as any one particular product is concerned. Therefore, I just do not see that there is anything that can be done to prevent a limited amount of United States pulpwood which happened to be in a given geographical situation, particularly in the Lake of the Woods area, where it can be marketed more readily and cheaply in Canada than in the United States because of its proximity to the paper mills, coming in to our markets.
There is no way of setting a price?

I would think it is extremely difficult to set a price for something which is imported from another country unless you put it under import control. If you did that, of course, it would lead immediately to retaliatory measures, and in the case of pulp and paper products it would certainly be to our terrific disadvantage.

Mr. Chairman, I have one question I would like to ask the minister. On May 10 various farm organizations presented a brief to him, and I am wondering if the minister will tell the committee if he has taken any steps toward meeting the requests made to him. If not, does he intend to write to those various farm organizations and reply to their requests, stating what he intends to do about them?
Is the hon. member referring to various poultry associations which came to see me?
Yes.

I told these people when they were here, and I have also stated this in reply to a question in the house, I believe this week although it may have been last week, that we would attempt at the next GATT negotiating conference to secure equalized rates as between ourselves and the United States as far as duties on poultry products are concerned.

Item agreed to.
11. Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, $62,667.

Mr. Chairman, in reviewing item No. 11, which is for a subsidy for cold storage, I am a little concerned about the sharp reduction in the amount of money available this year. Perhaps after I have spoken briefly on this matter the minister might be able to clarify it to some extent.
The matter of cold storage is very important to fruit and vegtable growing, which is the most important industry in the Niagara peninsula where I represent the county of Lincoln. I notice that the chairman has given a certain amount of leeway today and I am going to take advantage of that in saying to the minister that this year, as far as I know the only year for a long time, the fruit and vegetable growers in the Niagara peninsula have not presented a brief or petition or something like that in connection with dumping from the United States, which for so long has been their great problem. There have been changes in the regulations. The price stabilization act has been passed; there has been an extension of the seasonal tariff; and there has also been this matter of fair value for duty. However, in spite of all this the fruit growers still have problems, and one of their problems is the selling of their products. There is about 60 per cent-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Chair has been quite lenient so far but I hope the hon. member will come back to the item referring to cold storage.

Mr. Chairman, I was just about to come back to it. About 60 per cent of the crop goes for processing and 40 per cent to the basket trade, and the need for cold storage is very important for both of those ways of disposing of the crop.
In recent years there has been a sharp reduction in the number of canning factories which means that cold storage is very essential because sometimes the farmers have their crops ready to take to the plant but they

find the plant cannot handle them that day, or the following day, which means they have to put them into storage space. As you know, tender fruit and vegetables are very hard to take care of unless you have suitable cold storage acccommodation for them.
As far as the basket trade is concerned, I think the matter of cold storage is even more important because in years gone by most of that trade went to the corner grocery store or the home canner, but today it is sold to about six large buyers, the chain stores. They do not take it in small quantities; they like to get it in carloads which means that the fruit has to be stored for a certain length of time in order to supply their requirements. As I said, I am concerned about why the subsidy is reduced by so much this year and I am just wondering if the growers in the area are not taking full advantage of the subsidy available to them.
There is also the question of private cold storage. I quite admit that there is no subsidy available for that at the present time but I understand a great many of the larger growers in my area are considering something of that kind. I would like the minister to take that into consideration and make some kind of subsidy or grant available to the private family farmer who wishes to build a cold storage plant for himself.
Another thing which I would like to suggest to the minister concerns the preparing of plans and specifications for small cold storage plants. X think the experimental farm could help there, and we have a wonderful experimental farm in Lincoln county which could render great assistance to the growers in preparing plans and specifications of some kind. The growers in the Niagara peninsula have gone through some rather bad years; but everything looks much better now with new anti-dumping legislation and there is the possibility of the old family farms, the larger farms, coming back again. Therefore. I would certainly urge the minister to give this matter of cold storage very serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, this reduction is more apparent than is likely actually to be the case. The figures here are not really comparable. The figure of $433,510 was the final figure for the amount of cold storage subsidies. It has been the custom for some considerable time as far as this vote is concerned, to put in the amount of subsidy that will be required to pay for the applications which are already in and have been approved. In this case they happen to amount to this figure of $62,667. Since the original estimates were prepared before Christmas- some time last fall-there have been several other applications for subsidies which have
