been approved aggregating something over $190,000, I believe. Those will appear in the first supplementaries when they are introduced. I can assure the hon. member that any of these cold storages which qualify will be dealt with just as they have been in past years by supplementary estimates after the applications come in and have been approved.

Mr. Chairman, I have just received a letter from the Osoyoos co-operative fruit and vegetable growers in British Columbia in regard to cold storage. Apparently there is a new quality control regulation which has just been brought in the result of which will be to pay an additional 15 cents per box for possible costs to come in the future, provided the top cold storage requirements are met. I was wondering whether the department had received any correspondence in this regard because I can see that there will be a rather large request for further cold storage out in that area.
The letter I have received was written, as I say, by the Osoyoos co-operative fruit and vegetable growers who previously had a 10-year building plan in hand. They had been requesting that the department pass on their total plans for the next ten years. This letter informs me that because of the change in the quality control they are faced with asking for this cold storage subsidy to help in the development of an additional 40,000-box storage. Has the minister received any information in regard to this quality control within the Okanagan valley?

I have not received anything personally. My officials inform me they have no knowledge of any such request having come in. However, I should like to assure the hon. member that requests for cold storages on the part of co-operatives are always dealt with by us in as considerate a way as possible under the act. It would not be possible under the act to approve of a cold storage program which was to extend over the next ten years. Farmers' co-operatives that request assistance in building cold storages get first consideration and priority as far as we are concerned. It is only because we want to assist organizations of that kind that the act has not been repealed.

May I clear up one point, Mr. Chairman. This co-operative will be applying within the next few days. Due to the lateness of the season I hope I can have an assurance from the minister that everything possible will be done to speed up the processing of the application.

Supply-Agriculture
Yes, Mr. Chairman, we will certainly attempt to deal with it as expeditiously as possible and I can assure the hon. gentleman that we do this in all cases o 1 this kind.

Mr. Chairman, a little over a year ago a group of farmers in the lakehead became interested in trying to develop a cold storage plant there to take advantage of the operations of this act. They did not meet with success largely due to the fact in my judgment that they lacked experienced guidance and help. This brings up a question I have already brought to the minister's notice and on which I wish to speak later in another part of his estimates. I refer to the role played by the department in small isolated areas where because of the small number of farmers it is difficult to organize in such a way as to have the weight to take advantage of funds such as this and where it is difficult for these groups to acquire the necessary expertise.
Every time this brought to the minister's attention, probably through the advice of his officials, reference is made to it being a provincial matter, in essence, and to the fact that initiative should come from that source. The situation remains that our agricultural economy at the lakehead continues to drop. Appeals to provincial authorities do not appear to be effective. We do not seem to get the required leadership from the federal department in our region and we tend to be just a little saw-off of the Winnipeg offices of the department.
I was wondering if the minister could comment on this estimate of the situation and state whether or not he would agree that it is extremely difficult in an isolated region like ours to get a group together that can take advantage of this kind of legislation without much stronger leadership from the department.

Mr. Chairman, as I have noted on several occasions previously, extension work in agriculture is the field of the provinces. We have no organization or staff available to carry on extension work nor do we have an organization from which we could draw men to send to all parts of the country to organize farm groups whether it be for the purpose of building a cold storage warehouse, a cheese factory, a potato warehouse or something else. In the division of responsibility between the dominion and the provinces this is a responsibility of the provinces and not the dominion. We do not have the staff or organization to do it.
Could the minister say whether in the last year or two any money has been spent in the area west of the clay belts to the Manitoba border?
I am informed that we do not have the records here beyond last year but last year there was no cold storage subsidized in that area.

When I look at the provincial estimates and the pattern there I see a surprising number of these cold storage warehouses across the province of Ontario that have received support both under this and the provincial legislation but there seems to be a complete gap up in northern and northwestern Ontario. I urge the minister to have this situation examined and perhaps have a request sent to the provincial authorities asking them why there have been so few requests from that part of the country.

I think I would be going beyond what is generally regarded as acceptable conduct if I were to support putting pressure on the provincial government to do more extension work in a particular part of the province. I believe that would be looked upon as unwarranted interference on my part in a provincial responsibility. I cannot give the hon. gentleman the assurance for which he asks.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if the reason for that would be because it is now apparent that Premier Frost is not satisfied with the fiscal policy of the government?
That is a red herring.
Mr. Chairman, as usual the hon. member for Essex East is trying to introduce completely irrelevant red herrings.
That is not a red herring. It is a genuine question.

I want to underline the point I have made, Mr. Chairman, because in situation after situation, we cannot take advantage of this and other legislation due to our isolation. I am sure there have been no funds spent in our region under the stabilization act. There is hardly anything I can think of in the spending of this department that goes to the aid of our farmers because of their isolation.
I can cite an example from the pulpwood industry relating it to a portion of the agricultural marketing act of Ontario which contains a provision for support of co-operatives by the province. I took it up with a provincial minister and he said that he was not going to get himself involved in anything like that if he could help it; let sleeping dogs lie. While the minister's department is wait-

ing for the provincial department to take the initiative our little agricultural economy is collapsing. In so many aspects of the spending by the federal government the smaller places just have not a chance. It seems to me this requires a special effort, not only on the part of the smaller places themselves but on the part of people who have any ministerial responsibility. Even if the minister could do it unofficially will he just ask Mr. Goodfellow why it is that the provincial government is not taking any initiative in this particular item for our part of the country?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the position with reference to exports?

Last year, which was a bigger year for exports than we have had for a long time, we exported something in the neighbourhood of 17 to 18 million pounds, as I remember. I am not guaranteeing that to be the exact figure but it is in that neighbourhood. The exports this year have not been running as heavily as last year. However, I think we have every prospect of being able to export a very considerable amount of cheese; I would hope it might be very close to what we exported last year but it will have to be at lower prices.
The hon. member probably knows that last year the cheese producers got more for their cheese than they had ever got at any time in Canadian history. It just so happened that the very high price was to a large extent due to the drought in Europe last year which created a relative shortage of dairy products.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was the price of the cheese sold on the United Kingdom market?

Some of the cheese sold on the United Kingdom market was sold at prices somewhere between 40 cents and 44 cents a pound. This was last year during, as I say, a period when the price of dairy products

went up very rapidly and materially in Europe. At the present time cheese is being exported at about, I think, 32 cents a pound.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is most of it going to the United Kingdom?

Yes; we have no material exports anywhere else. The hon. member is probably aware that we have a quota of, I believe, 468,000 pounds of cheddar cheese in the United States, and that is all we are allowed to export to that country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Was that quota filled in 1959?
It was filled in 1959, yes.

On the subject of cheese, I understand that the GATT trading arrangement is up for renewal with the United States this year. Is it possible to increase the amount of cheese that we are sending to the United States? After all, half a million pounds is the make in my constituency alone of 10 days in any of the summer months. It is an insignificant amount to go to a very good market when one considers the overall production of the country. The population of the United States is over 180 million and certainly 500,000 pounds do not appear to be an advantageous amount to our cheese producers.
With respect to the questions asked by the hon. member for Laurier, I may perhaps be a little closer to the situation than is the minister because the five eastern countries of Ontario produced roughly 30 per cent of the total production of cheddar cheese manufactured in Canada in 1959. I believe the quantity of cheese that scored 92, 93 or 94 and thus commanded top prices and the bonus was a little better than 97 per cent.

I now have these figures. Exports of cheese last year were more than the figure I had in my mind. They were 20 million pounds rather than the figure of 17 to 18 million pounds that I gave. As to the scoring of cheese, cheese scoring 93 or more points in Quebec amounted to 59.34 per cent of their production and in Ontario cheese scoring 93 or more points amounted to 62.01 per cent in 1959.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott brought up a point which it seems to me is a very excellent one. If there is anyone in the house who knows the cheese situation I am sure it is he. He referred to increasing the export quota to the United States. We now have a number of committees on the ministerial level, the parliamentary level and also the business level in which United States representatives participate, the object of which is to iron out any problems or difficulties we

have with the United States. It seems to me that this might be an excellent opportunity to bring up on the ministerial level at least the increasing of the quota. If the position is as the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott states, and I am sure it is, that there could easily be a great increase in the production of cheese, then here is an opportunity to sell more cheddar cheese to that country. Would the minister give some consideration to the suggestion which has been thrown out?

Yes, this would be a very desirable thing if we could accomplish it. As I think the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott knows, I have made representations on several occasions particularly at ministerial meetings on economic affairs with ministers of the United States. Very strong representations have been made that the quota on cheddar cheese should be increased. We have not been given that but I hope that we may secure an improved quota over the one we have at the present time. Of course, I must say that whenever these matters are brought up the Americans point out that we have a complete ban on dairy products coming into this country and that we do not allow the entry of cheddar cheese or butter from any other country. Under these circumstances it is pretty difficult to say that they should increase their quota when we do not give them any quota at all.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to say a word or two about increasing the quota. I was in the United States some time ago and I noted that our Black Diamond cheese was selling for $1.59 a pound there. Some of that cheese came from my own area where it is purchased for 32 to 34 cents a pound. There is a market in the United States and I suppose our cheese commands a premium price because of the limited quota. I should like to ask the minister whether we have anybody in Great Britain who is attempting to promote the sale of our cheddar cheese there?

The answer to the hon. member's question is yes. The president of the Ontario cheese producers association is either over there or on his way over right now. This is also one of the things to which our agricultural counsellor in London gives constant attention.

Mr. Chairman, I want to bring a few matters to the minister's attention from the brief presented by the Thunder bay milk producers association to the agricultural marketing inquiry committee of Ontario. Premier Frost of Ontario has become quite a committee man in recent

years and has been sending all kinds of committees foraging around the province to get ideas. Kecently this committee visited the lakehead to find out just what the complaints of the farmers were and the milk producers submitted a brief which I can only say is an extremely pessimistic one, and with good reason because the farm decline in our part of the province has been astounding. I think it is proper to speak of it on this item because so much of the farming in our region is dairy farming.
It is apparent now that the quantity of improved land occupied and operated in the Thunder bay region has dropped phenomenally just as the population on the farms has dropped at a rate about ten times as great as in the other rural parts of the province. When the milk producers were through setting out their problems, competition from Manitoba, the very high costs of milk production in our area because of the long winter and short growing season, the scarcity of feed and other such factors, they wound up with a conclusion that I would hope will lead to a bit more initiative on the part of the provincial department of agriculture. They point out in their brief that they wish to emphasize that the farmers of the north require special help, assistance, understanding, leadership and support from the various departments of government, both provincial and federal, if they are to stay in the business of farming and to have the opportunity to provide a good standard of living for themselves and their families.
I know this is a platitudinous generality but it is a platitude with a tremendous amount of truth in it. If the provincial government does approach the federal government in connection with the problem of the dairy producers in our isolated region I would ask the minister to give the matter every attention. I know that he is not going to take any initiative on his part to enter into what he thinks is primarily a provincial matter, but if something should come from the provincial government in response to this complaint of the Thunder bay milk producers, I should like to have the assurance from him that he will seize that invitation much more boldly than is perhaps normal in his department.
I should like to ask another question. Would it be possible to have a salesman from the marketing branch sell cheese in Great Britain?

Mr. Chairman, the primary job of our agricultural counsellor, who is quite a high ranking officer in the high commissioner's office, is to promote the use and sale of our agricultural products in Great Britain. I do not know that the stationing 79951-0-259J
Supply-Agriculture
there permanently of somebody from the marketing branch would be anything more than a duplication of work that is already being carried on. At one time or another we have sent people over on special missions to iron out particular difficulties. In fact, I have done a little of that myself on each of the last two occasions when I have been in the United Kingdom, last fall and the fall before.

I certainly appreciate what the minister has done when he has been over there. I know he has promoted the sale of cheese. But I was thinking of 1953 when we were not selling any cheese to Great Britain. I happened to be at a dairy congress over there and at that time I met the dairy commissioner of Ontario who was at the meeting and also on a mission to sell cheese. I had the privilege of staying with him for a couple of weeks. We made some contacts and through the contacts we made at that time we succeeded in selling $10,000 worth of cheese inside of a week. That was the first cheese Canada had sold for some time and we have been selling cheese ever since. It seemed to me that the contacts he made at that time and the sales talk he put forward were responsible for the opening up of this cheese market again at that time, and perhaps if we had something of that sort, a man to assist the cheese producers to sell their cheese, it might create a little larger market in Great Britain for some of our surplus cheese.

16. Health of animals division (including the former administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act and Meat and Canned Foods Act, and the former animal pathology) -
Operation and maintenance including authority, notwithstanding the Financial Administration Act, to spend revenue received during the year from packers requiring special services, $8,778,641.

If I may, I should like to make a few brief comments on the health of animals division in the minister's department, and the work that they have been doing. I should like to commend them for the work they have been doing and are doing. I should like to say a few words, however, concerning one of the difficulties they have in connection with veterinarians. I refer to the difficulty in recruiting qualified personnel to look after the veterinary work right across Canada.
This brings me to the subject of a veterinary college in western Canada. As the committee may know, in 1958 there was a university committee set up to conduct an investigation of the feasibility of establishing such a college, and they came to the unanimous decision that

Supply-Agriculture
we needed one in western Canada. Unfortunately a meeting of the three provincial ministers of agriculture vetoed the idea for the time being. We feel that this was a very retrograde step on their part, certainly when one considers that of the veterinarians in western Canada, 36 per cent are working for the federal government. This represents a large proportion of the veterinarians, and this branch of the department is having a great deal of trouble in recruiting qualified personnel. The opposition to the establishment of a western veterinary college rests on the fact that the maximum number of students are not now taking advantage of the courses offered at Guelph or St. Hyacinthe. This view, however, does not take into account the long distance from western Canada at which these colleges are situated, nor does it take into consideration the differences in the problems with which we are confronted in veterinary medicine in western Canada as compared with eastern Canada.
In order to give hon. members some idea of the number of veterinarians which we have in western Canada, I may say that we have one for every 13,000 head of livestock as compared with the United States which has one for 20,000 head of livestock. Certainly, with the very much improved program we have for tuberculosis, brucellosis and Johne's disease in cattle right across the country, we are going to need a large number of qualified veterinarians and technicians, as well as other people associated with veterinary medicine.
I should like to make a suggestion to the minister, that the heads of the four western colleges should get together again and perhaps if the minister can induce the Canada Council to make a substantial grant of several hundred thousand dollars toward the formation of a new veterinary college in western Canada, then the provincial ministers might give further consideration to this question. Certainly if we are going to maintain our livestock industry as it should be maintained in western Canada, we are going to need these veterinarians. Certainly if we are going to maintain the general health, not only of the animals but of people as well, then we have to have more qualified veterinarians, and we have to have the technical knowledge in this country. I hope the minister will try to give this a push, either officially or unofficially. I am sure it will do a great deal for the livestock industry in western Canada.

The shortage of veterinarians is, as the hon. member for Jasper-Edson pointed out, a serious matter in Canada, particularly so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned. Had it not been

that we were able to recruit a considerable number of veterinarians from the United Kingdom and from some European countries we would not have had sufficient staff to carry on the activities which, under the various acts, we are required to carry on in the way of inspection facilities and so forth.
I was very disappointed when the four western universities, or perhaps their governments, decided not to go ahead with the construction of a western veterinary college. I certainly hope they will see fit to do that in the relatively near future. So far as a grant from the Canada Council is concerned, I would be a little doubtful whether the members of the Canada Council, except our representative from Alberta who is a rancher and represents the livestock and agriculture industry generally, would look upon a veterinary college as a cultural activity.

I am not quite sure whether I am in order, but I think I am approximately in order. I want to say a word or two about a matter that does concern an increasing number of my constituents who are interested in the raising of beef cattle. I may say, for the information of the minister, that there has been a considerable increase in the population of beef cattle in the Kootenay West area, particularly in some of the isolated valleys. When I tell him that I know of one valley that has 16,000 acres of first class grazing land which are, as yet unused, he may understand the possibilities for development in the future.
However the West Kootenay and central farmers institute, and I think the deputy minister of agriculture in British Columbia, have had some correspondence with the health of animals branch with respect to getting Nel-way designated as a port of import and export for Canada. I took this matter up with the minister in February, and he kindly informed me that Nelway is designated for the inspection of cattle, but that it is entirely up to the United States authorities whether or not they agree to have their port designated for the export of cattle. I fully appreciate that situation, but I would ask the minister and his officials to keep the matter in mind, knowing that there is still great interest in this question. It is a great inconvenience to those who ship cattle from West Kootenay or from the eastern portion of East Kootenay to ship through other ports. I trust the department will keep the matter in mind, and if there is an opportunity to persuade the United States authorities that they would be justified in taking this action it would be very much appreciated by those people who are raising beef cattle in my constituency and in the surrounding area.

I recall this case. I remember the United States authorities took the position, which I could not say was not justified, that there was not sufficient traffic through this point to justify the maintenance of a regular inspection service. However, if there was need for inspection, say every two weeks or once a month, they would consider providing that inspection service. The amount of traffic is very small, and it does not justify them having a man there; there is no question about that.

Would I be correct in suggesting to the beef producers that if they could make some arrangement to ship at a certain time, and notify the authorities, it might be possible to have an arrangement made with the United States authorities?
Under these circumstances I think we could make arrangements with the United States veterinary service to have somebody there to make an inspection.

That comprises the $265,200?
Yes, for building.

In the matter of an estimate for the construction of buildings or for that matter in any estimate, it is rather unusual that the precise amount asked for in the previous year should be asked for in the current year. Does this represent careless estimating? Is this not an indication perhaps that the government is not taking the steps with regard to retrenchment which we were assured were taken? In any event, I think the committee is entitled to an explanation of why the precise amounts are covered for the two fiscal years.
Supply-Agriculture

Again, most of the construction moneys provided for were revotes which were in last year. Apart from that fact, the reason for this is that treasury board reduced our requests by a considerable amount here and brought them down to the same amount that we had provided for last year. We were obliged to distribute the money on that basis. That is the explanation of their being brought down to this point. We had actually asked and put in an estimate for a larger amount than that which appears.

I can understand how you could have the same amount if you were giving a grant to some organization; but where it is a question involving the construction of buildings, unless you propose to leave out a door or not instal a bathroom, I cannot understand the situation.
I think the hon. member does not realize that this vote takes in equipment as well as construction; and the equipment is the item particularly which has been cut down.
The explanation is not too satisfactory but I suppose we shall be obliged to accept it.
When a building is contemplated is any plan or estimate made by the department before they go to the treasury board to ask for the money?

Yes, of course, we have a plan. We have a plan for, say, public buildings A, B, C, D and E. We put them in the estimates and the treasury board may insist that we take out one or two of them, thereby cutting down the amount.

Is there not any fixed estimate as to what such a building or such equipment would cost? How is it possible to cut it down without looking at the estimate? That is, how is it possible to cut it down to the very same amount it was the year previous without looking at the estimate?

As to equipment, you can adjust it down almost in any way you wish. You just buy that much less equipment of various kinds. We put in a certain amount for equipment and treasury board says, "You will have to get by with less equipment and get this vote down to not more than it was last year". That is the position in which we found ourselves.

We take in a part or percentage of the money wagered. One half of one per cent of the money wagered comes to us. In return for that money we provide race track supervision including eye in the sky, the testing of horses, saliva test and so on.

What is eye in
the sky?

It is a camera device which follows the race right around. By looking at the film it can be determined whether the jockeys did anything which was illegal and so forth. It is a means of ensuring to the general public that the race has been run completely fairly. Also, of course, it determines at the finish line, by photographic means, exactly which horse won.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word here about the 4-H movement, which comes under this item. 1 understand that the 4-H movement had its roots in the gardens of our rural schools more than 40 years ago. From that humble beginning the organization as we know it gradually evolved, and today numbers 75,854 boys and girls. Many thousands of people on farms or in jobs related to agriculture acknowledge their debt to their early association with 4-H. The governments, both federal and provincial, are solidly behind 4-H because the value of its educational, vocational and social activities has been amply proved. The care of livestock, knowledge of crop cultivation, particularly the value of good seed, and on the distaff side, homemaking with special reference to rural life, are among the subjects taught which are most closely related to the farm. Other less tangible assets derived from 4-H work, but of paramount importance, are leadership, ability to work alone and with a group, making decisions, public speaking and citizenship.
As we well know, the federal government last year broadened its own farm loan program and in setting up the Farm Credit Corporation made special provision for loans to capable farmers as young as 21 years of age. If such a farmer has sufficient equity and qualifications he can get a loan as high as $27,500 for the purchase of a farm. Such a loan would cost only 5 per cent in interest and the period of repayment could be stretched to 30 years if necessary. Of course the lending authority would have to be satisfied that the enterprise and the plan of operation bore reasonable promise of success, but this is to the advantage of the borrower as well as ensuring that the public money will be repaid. Loans are made up to 75 per cent of the assessed value of the farm and every assistance is given by the local district officer of the Farm Credit Corporation In preparing and presenting loan applications. I mention this to demonstrate that our government is confident that there is a great future on the land for those citizens who prepare themselves for such a career.
At the 4-H stage we are concerned that the young folk develop a love of farm life, or at least an appreciation of the part the farmer plays in the structure of the nation. There are more than 20 agricultural and home economics projects in which the children may engage. They learn good practices at an age when they have not had time to

Private Bills-Divorce learn bad practices. Some of them have appeared at provincial forums and in recent years the representatives of each province have been our unofficial ambassadors in the United States, meeting their opposite numbers and seeing something of the great agricultural organization set up by our neighbour farmers across the line.
Graduates of 4-H find themselves at the threshold of a variety of careers. They may continue as junior farmers and carry into practice with their own stock and crops the knowledge they have gained from others. Many go into technical schools for training and some enter universities and eventually become professional men in one of the various fields open to young people today. It is very pleasing to record that some of the best leaders in 4-H work have been recruited from the ranks of junior farmers in Ontario and, in other provinces where there is no equivalent organization, from the graduates of 4-H clubs.
In Waterloo county I am told that there were 212 4-H projects completed in 1959. Of these, 132 were in calf clubs, 38 in swine clubs, 10 in a poultry club, 19 in a tractor club and 13 in a conservation club.

We can see from this brief reference to the evidence that this case is unlike so many other cases. There is no great difficulty involved. There are no arguments and no one gets angry at the investigators. It appears to be quite a normal thing for the respondent to want to participate in such an event. Perhaps he too expected such action was forthcoming and that if, as is given in the evidence, he and the corespondent were living as man and wife he could expect almost daily that something of this nature would occur and that divorce proceedings would be be initiated. I would imagine that anyone in similar circumstances could reasonably be expected to think in somewhat the same terms

As I said before, the evidence given here shows that circumstances existed which could reasonably be interpreted as indicating either that adultery had taken place or might reasonably be expected to take place. That is also corroborated extensively by the reference to the respondent and corespondent living as man and wife in a common law arrangement when in fact they were not married. Probably this is sufficient in itself to be acceptable as proof of adultery. I understand that evidence of this nature would be completely acceptable in a court of law, that the evidence is quite acceptable where it appears that a situation exists where a couple are living together as man and wife and in fact this is considered to be grounds for a divorce even though some slight reference must be made to adultery by indicating that there is a bedroom, that the pillows have both been used and the bed is mussed up and that there is only one bed. It would seem, of course, that we should give different degrees of weight, as I am sure a court would do, to different types of evidence and different circumstances. If, for argument's sake, evidence had been adduced that this couple had visited a hotel or motel where they had registered for only one night, perhaps additional corroborative evidence would be needed by the courts and by the committee of the other place to establish the necessary proof.
I have no further comments to make, Mr. Chairman. I am quite sure that in this instance, as was indicated by the hon. member for Halifax, there is no conflict in the evidence of the investigators apart from a 10 or 15-minute time difference which actually means nothing. There appears to be no reference to invasion of the rights of individuals such as we find in other cases, that is, evidence of investigators forcing themselves into someone's premises. They walked in and we might assume that there was some form of invitation or acquiescence at least on the part of the respondent. In short, this is one of those cases where we probably cannot engage in too much discussion.

The evidence of the committee can certainly be used in the house in any way an hon. member wishes to do so. He may read it, discuss it or refer to it.

I am attempting to have this particular point clear because I think there is some doubt in my mind as to whether or not it is permissible under the ruling to make reference to the evidence taken before the committee of the other place, even though the subject matter to which that evidence refers is beyond our jurisdiction here.

May I speak briefly to the point of order? I thought the previous rulings were to the effect that we could read the evidence, even ad nauseam of the Senate divorce committee on a particular case, if the matters that were read or if the matters that were discussed there were relevant to the bill under consideration. I think that is the obvious point of distinction that should be drawn. I think it would be improper for us to deal with matters relating to the children which are matters of court procedure in the province of Quebec and, therefore, not really matters under the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament in considering a divorce bill.
I think that point of order has been raised before and I think there is a clear answer to my hon. friend about reading from reports. Yes, it may be done if it is relevant to the issue before us.

Before you do rule, Mr. Chairman, may I make one more comment about this. It raises another matter and perhaps I can put this, not as a point of order but as a question with which you may deal. When the hon. member for Halifax opened the discussion on this bill he made a reference to the economic position of the petitioner and stated the income which she was receiving. I wonder whether Your Honour would rule, also, whether or not such a reference is germane to the bill before us.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Of course, in ruling on the question of children, I made it very plain before that the evidence given before the committee of the other place may be used here if it is relevant to the bill before us. I thought I had made that plain, and I believe that answers the other question as well.

I take it, Mr. Chairman, that hereinafter we cannot deal with the income of an individual or his economic or other circumstances. I had intended to follow along, because the hon. member for Halifax had done so, in making a slight reference to the income of this petitioner in this particular instance and the sufficiency of it for herself. As I agree with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, which is now clarified fairly well, we will dispense with that particular reference.
Some difficulties arose prior to this time. Perhaps I could make reference to them. This is with respect to their living together and cohabiting:
Q. Until when did you live with your husband?
A. Until January three years ago.
Q. Would that be January 1957?
A. Yes.
Q. What happened at that time?
A. He left our home towards the end of January.
Q. Had you taken any action in the courts?
A. Yes.
Q. Was it as a result of the action he left your home?
A. Yes.
Q. Prior to that what was the situation in your home?
This answer gets to the relevant part of it.
A. About a year and a half after our marriage he began to mistreat me very badly both mentally and physically.
Q. What do you mean mistreated you physically?
A. He beat me.
Q. How often did that happen?
A. Very often, at least two or three times a week.
Q. What finally happened?
A. Finally one evening he beat me so badly that he burst open my ear.
Q. Did you get assistance at that time?
A. No. I was too ashamed to mention it.
Q. Did you ever have to call anybody into the house in connection with these beatings?
A. I did not because I had a full-time housekeeper who heard this last beating.
Q. I was thinking of the police or something of that nature.
A. Oh yes, I did call the police on one occasion.
Private Bills-Divorce
If this young lady, the petitioner here, and her husband had been living in the province of Nova Scotia, I am sure they would have had no difficulty in obtaining a divorce on the evidence given here. It seems odd that people in one province have different opportunities for divorce from those of people in another province.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Order.
Perhaps our federal laws should be altered accordingly so that there is uniformity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Order.
Continued attempts to disregard the Chair.

speechtext: Order.

May I say this? When the chairman calls to my attention the fact that perhaps I am not strictly following the rules, I invariably bow to his suggestions.
On page 10 there is some reference to whether there was any understanding or agreement. The following questions were asked by Mr. Lieff:
Q. Is there any agreement or understanding between you and your husband to get this divorce?
A. None whatsoever.
Q. Do you know what the word connive means?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you connived at the adultery or schemed about it or planned it in any way?
A. No.
Q. Is there any chance of a reconciliation between you and your husband?
A. None whatsoever.
Q. If you had more time do you think you could rebuild this marriage?
A. No, we had plenty of time and I feel that we are both too mature to change.
Then there is reference to the child which you, Mr. Chairman, say is not relevant. Then we find the following questions:
Q. Have you forgiven him for the adultery which you complain about in the petition?
A. I have not.
Q. Do you know a-
And here is given the name of the corespondent.
A. No.
Q. Were you with your husband on September 9 1959?
A. No.
Q. Have you had marital relations with him since the separation?
A. No.
Q. How long did you know him before you were married?
A. One year.
Q. Was there any indication during that period that perhaps this marriage might not succeed?
A. No.
Then follows a question about the respondent's use of another name and Mr. Lieff

Private Bills-Divorce
makes a motion, which is granted, that the petition be altered also to read accordingly. Then Mr. Daigneault is called as a witness. He is an investigator and Mr. Lieff poses questions to him. He identifies a photograph as being that of the respondent. Then the following questions are asked by Mr. Lieff:
Q. Did you investigate his behaviour?
A. I did, sir.
Q. Over what period of time?
A. Our services being retained by Mr. McKay of Montreal during the early part of August, 1959, at which time Mr. McKay furnished us with this photograph.
I assume that Mr. McKay is another barrister or solicitor in the city of Montreal and that Mr. Lieff is, in fact, what is known as an agent or working with Mr. McKay. Then we find the following:
Q, Exhibit 2?
A. That's right, sir, and also giving us certain instructions. I verified those particulars and found them to be true and as a result of the investigation, on September 9, 1959, accompanied by Mr. Paquette we proceeded to-
There is given here the address in Montreal and the apartment number. The answer continues as follows:
-where after ringing the bell a few times the door was answered by-
Here is given the name of the respondent.
-at which time he was wearing a maroon dressing gown, slippers, and bare legs.
I identified myself to him and we walked into the apartment and I told him why I was there,-
You will notice, Mr. Chairman, the ease with which this takes place. There is no question of asking whether they can go in. He says:
I identified myself and we walked into the apartment and I told him why I was there, and on the righthand side of the back of the apartment was a pulled-out studio couch in which the woman was lying on the far side near the wall. That woman answered to the name of Mrs.-
There is given here a surname which is the same as that of the respondent. The answer continues:
-when I went to the door previously. I went to the bed and asked her her name and she hesitated a few moments and then she answered-
Here is given the name of the corespondent. The answer continues:
I asked her her address and she said, "I am living here". We told both of them they would be hearing from his real wife's attorney in the near future, and we left afterwards.
Q. How was that woman clothed?
A, When X went to speak to her she was in a kind of sitting position and she was at least in the top part of pink pyjamas.
Q. How many beds in that room?
A. That was the only sleeping accommodation in the whole apartment.
Q. What was its condition?
A. The left-hand side seemed to have been previously occupied because there was an impression on the pillow.

Q. Please look at the petitioner. Was she the woman you saw there on that occasion?
A. No sir, I never saw this woman there.
By Senator Bradley:
Q. This woman,-
Here is given the name of the corespondent.
-was in bed when you saw her?
A. Yes.
By Mr. Lieff:
Q. What hour was that?
A. Approximately midnight.
At this point I should like to mention one thing I noticed immediately which appeared to be at variance with the usual method of giving evidence in these cases. I refer to the fact that in the initial part of his evidence Mr. Daigneault makes no reference to the time at which they appeared at this particular apartment. It will be noticed that in other cases it is always 11.15 or 11.35 or 12.30 or whatever the actual time of the day it might be. In his initial evidence I think perhaps Mr. Daigneault, he being quite experienced in these matters, could have cleared that point up immediately unless, of course, he had lost his mimeographed slip from which these gentlemen give this stereotyped evidence. In any event, they finally got around to saying that this was the hour of approximately midnight.
Would the hon. member permit a question on a point of information. Does he not realize that witnesses are not allowed to read from statements in the Senate? They can refer to notes.

Yes. Perhaps in this case they were mimeographed notes. All I say is, Mr. Daigneault is apparently quite a competent, able and thoroughly experienced investigator, and surely after this period of time has come to know his role full well and to give evidence in that fashion of times and everything else. It did seem a little odd why this was not done previously. Then the chairman, Senator Cameron, intervenes and asks:
Q. Did it seem like they had been living there?
A. I asked Mr.-"Are you living here with this woman?" And he said "Yes, I have been living here with this woman for the past month or so".
By Senator Bradley:
Q. She heard that?
A. Yes.
Q. And she made no objection to it?
A. No.
In this instance the circumstances are similar to those in the other case except that the common law arrangement here is tied down to a period, "for the past month or so".
Mr. Paquette then appeared as a witness. He was sworn and asked certain questions by Mr. Lieff about identification of the photograph.
Q. Did you make any inquiries about him at any time?

A. On September 9, 1959, I accompanied Mr. Daigneault to his apartment, apartment 4, at- Montreal.
Q. At what time of the day?
A. It was about five minutes before twelve when we arrived there. Mr. Daigneault rang the bell and Mr.-opened the door. We identified ourselves and we went into the apartment. Once we were in the apartment he showed him this picture.
Q. He showed whom?
A. Mr.-
Q. The picture, exhibit 2?
A. Yes. sir. He admitted it was his picture. So, due to the fact it was only a one and a half room apartment we noticed right away there was a woman in the studio couch.
By Senator Bradley:
Q. It was then a bed, was it? What you call a studio couch was then arranged as a bed?
A. A double bed, yes. So at that time Mr. Daigneault asked her who she was and she said her name was-
Giving the name of the corespondent.
By Mr. Lieff:
Q. How was she dressed?
A. She sat in the bed and she had on the top of, it could be, baby doll pyjamas.
Q. What was the condition of the bed?
A. The bed was disturbed. You could see it had been used by two persons.
Q. How was Mr.-dressed?
A. He had a dressing gown on and it was open and you could see his bare legs and a pair of slippers.
Q. How many beds in the room?
A. Just the one double bed.
Q. Please look at the petitioner. Was she the woman you saw there then?
A. No, sir.
Q. Was there any conversation other than what you have told us?
A. We told Mr.-the reason we were there and that Mrs.-was taking a divorce.
Q. Did you find out how long-had been living there?
A. No, I don't remember.
Here again, Mr. Chairman, we have an indication of a common law alliance, although just where you draw the line between a casual acquaintance and a situation which will result in them being able to say they are living together as man and wife, I do not know. In this instance Mr. Daigneault
Business of the House
indicated that they had been living there together for the past month or so.
This may be an interesting point that the judiciary has ruled upon or developed some case law on, namely as to when a relationship between a man and a woman who are not married changes from that of being a casual one to one in which you can say a common law arrangement exists. I only raise this point because I think the courts and undoubtedly the committee of the other place as well as this committee here would give more weight to a petition for divorce where there was in fact a common law or man and wife living arrangement than they might to the question whether there was an actual opportunity for adultery to take place.
Perhaps I might refer briefly to other cases by way of comparison. There is the evidence given in other cases where hotels or motels are involved, where they go to some length to talk about the state of the clothing and the condition of the bed, and the time element-waiting till the lights go out and all that sort of thing-in order to show that reasonable opportunity existed for adultery to take place.
